bugs: PushStockAllocations has no retryUntil, only #[Tries(10)] (Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:16). A 429 can release the job for up to 600s each time (line 49), and backoffs are 30/120/300s, so retries can run well past the 15-minute claim TTL. The dispatcher then re-claims rows that are still in flight and dispatches a second job, which can mean duplicate pushes. When the old job finally calls failed(), it clears the new job's claim (line 73).
The job never filters disabled_at (line 34-37). A row disabled after it was claimed is still POSTed and then marked synced. Probe P3 confirmed this.

Same-second race: synced_at = $startedAt uses second precision. An edit landing in the same second as the read, but after it, leaves updated_at == synced_at, so the change is never pushed. Probe P1 confirmed this.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:16 sets a fixed Tries(10) on a job whose 429 releases count as attempts. Nothing ties the retry window to the claim TTL.
app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:45 calls asJson(), which is redundant because post() with an array already sends JSON.
app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php:23 hardcodes the 'redis' store name with Schedule::useCache('redis') instead of relying on the configured default cache.
tests/Feature/StockAllocationTest.php:63 uses isSameDay, a weak assertion that would not catch updated_at being bumped by a few seconds.
There is no test for the retry window against the claim TTL. That is exactly the gap the bug above falls into.
strengths: The dispatcher is the simplest of the four: chunkById over the readyToSync scope, which is safe even though the claim changes the filtered columns, plus a toBase() update so updated_at is not bumped.
The job only sends rows that are still claimed (whereNotNull sync_started_at), so a redelivered job does not resend. Probe P4 passed.
The sync and disable writes are wrapped in a transaction. It uses modern attributes (#[Scope], #[Fillable], queue and console attributes).

There is no proactive rate limiting. It only reacts to 429 with release(), so with three workers pulling 50 jobs it will keep hitting the limit.

retryUntil is derived from CLAIM_TTL_MINUTES - 1, which ties the retry window to the abandonment window in code. failed() frees the claim.

v.rationale:
I ranked them impl-3, impl-4, impl-2, impl-1. All four test suites pass (impl-2: 16, impl-3: 24, impl-4: 17, impl-1: 20 tests). All four share the same core design: a readyToSync scope, claiming with a toBase() update so updated_at is not bumped, onOneServer()->withoutOverlapping(), and a failed() hook that frees the claim. The ranking comes down to how each one handles the task's risks: rate limits, keeping the retry window under the 15-minute claim TTL, and duplicate or lost pushes.

I ran eight probes against each implementation and then deleted them:
- P1: an edit landing in the same second as an in-flight request.
- P2: a 429 with no Retry-After header.
- P3: a row disabled after it was claimed.
- P4: the job delivered a second time after it already succeeded.
- P5: a 200 response with an empty body.
- P6: 5,000 rows, expecting 50 unique jobs and nothing on the second run.
- P7: the job's retry window compared with the claim TTL.
- P8: a missing SKU staying disabled even after a later edit.

**impl-3 (rank 1)** is the only one that throttles before hitting the limit: RateLimited middleware on the shared Redis limiter, as well as handling 429 through tooManyRequests(). It writes in a transaction and keeps retries inside 10 minutes. Recording the claim time as synced_at means it is the only one that does not lose the same-second in-flight edit (P1). Its tests use the modern withFakeQueueInteractions()/assertReleased(). Against that, it resends when a job is delivered twice (P4), builds a small piece of raw SQL by string interpolation, and lists the state columns as fillable.

**impl-4 (rank 2)** only touches rows that are still claimed and enabled, so a second delivery after success is a no-op. That matters for the "exactly once" requirement on SQS, which delivers at least once. Its retry window is also bounded under the TTL. The minuses: legacy and redundant idioms (scopeX, #[UseFactory] plus $model, property-style queue config, a hardcoded endpoint), no transaction around the writes, and it loses the same-second edit.

**impl-2 (rank 3)** has the cleanest and most idiomatic code: attributes, partition(), and retryUntil derived from the claim TTL. But it resends on a second delivery (P4) and loses the same-second edit (P1), with no throttling beyond reacting to 429. It is a close call with impl-4. I put impl-4 ahead because it actually guards against duplicates, which the task's focus asks for.

**impl-1 (rank 4)** has the simplest dispatcher (chunkById) and a claim guard. Its real bug is #[Tries(10)] with no retryUntil, while each 429 release can wait up to 600s. Retries can therefore outlive the 15-minute claim, so the dispatcher sends the same rows again, and the old job's failed() later clears the new job's claim. It also sends rows that were disabled after being claimed (P3) and loses the same-second edit.
